author: Forbes
description:
What made the rapid downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—the star of the AI boom and one of the world’s richest people—all the more stunning was that it revealed he lacked the modern control of his company that other larger-than-life tech founders, through super-voting ownership shares, can exert to prevent such a total loss of power.

That’s because the chipmaker went public in 1999. Five years later two young Stanford computer scientists went to bankers with an unusual request about the public listing of their red-hot startup. Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin wanted their extraordinary control over the then startup to continue when it became a public company. 

The wunderkinds got what they asked for: dual-class shares that gave them 10 votes for every one share when the search giant went public in 2004. author: Forbes
description:
How does a single hot dog cart in a New York City park become a global, multi-billion-dollar empire? Forbes' Chase Peterson-Withorn sits down with restaurateur Danny Meyer, founder of Union Square Hospitality Group and Shake Shack. Meyer shares the story of how a humble hot dog cart designed to fund a local park turned into a multi-billion dollar global empire. He breaks down his framework for scaling a culture, the biggest trap leaders fall into when trying to grow (the "Shack Trap"), and why trusting your gut is the ultimate business hack.

author: Forbes
description:
In 1984, Jim Koch walked away from a $250,000-a-year consulting job to pursue a risky dream: brewing beer using a century-old family recipe. Armed with his savings, a second mortgage, and a belief that Americans deserved better beer, Koch launched Samuel Adams and helped revolutionize the American beer industry.

Four decades later, Boston Beer Company is a multibillion-dollar business, and Koch is worth an estimated $1.4 billion. Here's how he built his fortune by challenging the industry's biggest players—and why he still flies coach and drives a 2013 Ford Fusion.
